children.text: Quick answer:

a simple landing page for a repair shop costs €700-1,400. A conversion-focused site with full search and maps optimisation starts from €2,000. A multi-page site with individual service pages, a price calculator and booking starts from €2,000, and a redesign of an existing site from €1,000.
The final figure depends on the number of services, how quotes are produced, and integration with your shop management system.
What decides the return isn't the design — it's price transparency and how easy the first contact is.

Customers of repair shops carry a fear that most other trades don't produce: being taken advantage of. Unnecessary work added, a part replaced when it could have been repaired, one figure quoted on the phone and another at collection. That fear governs how drivers choose a shop, and everything the website does either removes it or reinforces it.
Which leads to the point: a repair shop's website sells predictability, not quality — everyone claims quality. Here's what such a site costs and what actually drives enquiries.
What determines the price of a repair shop website
The number of services and how they're structured.

A general shop, a marque specialist and a narrow operation like wheel restoration or gearbox rebuilds represent very different page counts. Every service you want to be found for needs a page of its own.
How quotes are produced.
A simple enquiry form, a price table, a parameter-based calculator or photo-based estimates are solutions of entirely different complexity and entirely different return.
Integrations.
A connection to your shop management system or CRM so bookings aren't duplicated by hand, order status lookup, deposit payments.
Local search.
For a shop with premises this isn't optional: structured data, correct address and hours markup, area pages, and a connection between the site and your maps listing.
Language versions.
In cities with a large international population, these open up customers your competitors aren't reaching at all.
Which auto repair website features actually generate enquiries
A few things work noticeably harder than the rest in this trade, and it's worth understanding why.
Transparent pricing.

A price list by job, or at least ranges, removes the central fear. Silence about price doesn't protect you from competitors — it attracts calls from people who were never going to book and deters the ones who were.
Photo-based estimates.

The feature that changes enquiry volume more than any other here. The customer photographs the damage, sends it through the form and gets an indicative price and timeline without driving over for an inspection. It removes the main friction: having to spend half a day to find out an approximate figure.
A parameter-based calculator.
Where cost follows from clear inputs, the estimate can be handed to the customer. They get a number immediately, and you get an enquiry from someone who already accepts the order of magnitude.
Order status lookup.
The customer enters a reference and sees what's happening with the vehicle and when it'll be ready. It takes the "any news?" calls off your front desk and noticeably improves the experience.
Accurate opening hours.
A small thing, but wrong hours on a site are worse than none: someone drives over to a closed gate. A live status indicator solves it.
Click-to-call and a short form.

On mobile, a call button fixed to the bottom of the screen outperforms every other conversion element. The form should ask for the minimum: contact details, make and model, a short description of the problem.
Three tiers of an auto repair shop website and what each includes
Simple landing page — €700-1,400

One page on a solid technical base: services, prices, contacts, an enquiry form, a map. Right when the task is minimal — establishing a presence, having a link for your listing, collecting enquiries from ads.

What isn't here: individual service pages, and therefore no visibility for specific jobs. This kind of page doesn't compete for searches like "clutch replacement" or "wheel refurbishment" — it's for people who already know where they're going.
Conversion site — from €2,000

The same format, built as an acquisition channel. Everything the simple version lacks is added: technical SEO and structured data, local business markup for map results, a structure designed around the enquiry, quote handling, and readiness for AI search.
The difference between €700 and €2,000 isn't page count — it's whether people who don't yet know you can find the site at all.
Multi-page site — from €2,000

For a shop with a broad range of work. Everything from the previous tier plus structure: a page for each service — which creates entry points from search for specific jobs — a gallery of completed work, area pages, a booking system with synchronisation, and an admin panel where you change prices and add services yourself.
Redesign of an existing site — from €1,000
If the site exists but produces no enquiries, a full rebuild isn't always necessary. Restructuring, adding quote handling and local optimisation on the existing base is often enough.
Case study: rebuilding a repair shop website and the result
The clearest example from my own work is Felgilab,
a Warsaw workshop specialising in alloy wheel restoration
. Their site ran on the ageing MODX platform: slow, with no conversion elements, and awkward for staff to update.

I rebuilt it on a custom WordPress theme — no page builders, no heavy plugin stack. The verified outcome: mobile performance went from around 50 to 92, the site now runs in four languages, and it gained a parameter-based price calculator, order status lookup by phone number, and a live open/closed indicator.

But the decisive change was something else. The enquiry form gained photo upload: the customer photographs the damaged wheels, sends them, and receives an estimate and a timeline. That single feature changed the flow of enquiries more than anything else — the large majority of visitors now attach photographs to their enquiry.
The lesson worth taking from it: the return came not from the rebuild itself, but from one feature aimed precisely at how customers in this trade make their decision.
Comparing the tiers of a repair shop website by price and purpose
Simple landing page
— €700-1,400 — Minimal task, traffic from ads or a listing — Almost nothing — competes only for your own name
Conversion site
— from €2,000 — A shop that needs enquiries from search and maps — Local search, map results, AI assistants
Multi-page site
— from €2,000 — Broad range of services, several specialisms — Individual searches per service and per area
Redesign
— from €1,000 — Site exists but brings no enquiries — Depends on the starting point — often a marked improvement
Maps listings, aggregators and your own repair shop website
A large share of repair shop customers arrive through map results and aggregator platforms, and there's no sense abandoning them. But the model has limits worth understanding.

A maps listing shows an address, hours and reviews — and that's where the information ends. Someone looking for a specific job can't tell from a listing whether you do it, what it costs or how long it takes. They keep looking.
Aggregators bring volume, but you pay per contact and sit beside competitors where the choice is made on price. The data and the repeat business stay with the platform.

Your own site replaces neither. It does something different: it answers the specific questions a listing can't, and it connects with your maps profile in both directions — the site strengthens the listing, the listing strengthens the site.
What else affects the final cost of an auto repair website
Content.
Photographs of your work and service descriptions — yours, or you need help. In this trade real photographs of your own jobs persuade more than any copy, and they're worth investing in separately.
Shop system integration.
If bookings live in a management system, connecting it removes manual duplication but adds scope.
Language versions.
Each is not just translation but a separate SEO structure.
Timeline.
A relaxed schedule is more economical than a rushed one.
How I build websites for auto repair shops
I combine development and SEO, so the service structure, local optimisation and technical base are designed together.
My experience in this trade is backed by a public case: a full rebuild of a Warsaw workshop's site,
migrated off an ageing platform
, with mobile performance up from around 50 to 92 and features that genuinely changed the flow of enquiries.
The sequence: we establish what work you do and how customers currently reach you; I design the structure and the quoting method; then development with local SEO and markup; then launch and support.
Where to start building an auto repair shop website
Reduced to one principle: a repair shop's website works when someone can tell within a minute whether you do the job they need, roughly what it costs, and how quickly you'll reply.

Start not with design but with the list of jobs you want more of. Those become individual pages and the backbone of the structure. Then the quoting method, because that's what removes the customer's central fear.
If you'd like to know what your current site is missing, write to me and we'll look at it together.

children.text: Quick answer:

a simple landing page for a construction company costs €700-1,400. A conversion-focused site with search and local optimisation starts from €2,000. A multi-page site with separate project pages, service pages and service areas starts from €2,000, and a redesign of an existing site from €1,000.
The price depends on how many trades you cover, the size of your portfolio, and whether you work with private clients, commercial ones, or both.
Enquiries come not from the design but from the work you show and the fear you remove.

In construction the client decides differently from most trades. They pay substantial sums up front, often before seeing any result at all, and their main fear isn't overpaying — it's being left with an unfinished build and a contractor who has disappeared. So the website works less as a showcase and more as evidence that you exist, have been working for years, and finish what you start.
Here's what such a site costs and what genuinely affects the number of enquiries.
What determines the price of a construction company website
The number of trades you cover.
General building, finishing, roofing, facades, mechanical services — every trade you want to be found for needs its own page describing the work, timelines and how pricing is approached.
The size of your portfolio.
Completed projects are the primary content in this field, and their number drives the scope. Every significant project deserves a page of its own.
Who your client is.
A private client building a house and a developer choosing a main contractor are two different paths through the site. If you serve both, that's effectively two sections with different logic.
Your service area.
Pages for the towns and districts you actually work in are a working tool in construction, because that's how people search.
How quotes are requested.
A simple form, a structured request capturing project parameters, the ability to attach drawings or photographs — different levels of effort and different quality of incoming enquiries.
Project pages: the main source of enquiries in construction
This is the section the site exists for in this field, and also the one most often done wrong.
The typical mistake is a single gallery captioned "project in the local area". It answers no search query and tells a client very little.

What works instead is a separate page per significant project. What the starting point was, what the brief required, which materials and solutions were chosen and why, how long it took, what difficulties came up. A page like that captures queries competitors don't have, and at the same time does what no gallery can — it shows how you think and how you run a site.

A note on photography. Photos from the building site don't sell; before-and-after does. The difference is fundamental: a client looks at a stripped plot and beside it a finished house, and immediately sees what they're paying for. One such block persuades more than five paragraphs about experience and professionalism.
How to remove the client's main fear: trust on a construction website
In this field trust isn't a soft factor but a condition of the contract. What builds it:
Licences, certifications and liability insurance.
Displayed prominently rather than buried in an "about us" page. For a client this is the first filter.
The contract and payment structure.
How the stages work, what sums are due when, what happens if there's a delay. A company that explains this before the phone call removes the main objection before it forms.
Reviews tied to specific projects.
"Client X, house in Y" carries far more weight than anonymous praise. Linking the profiles where you already hold reviews helps too.
Real people.
Photographs of the crew, the site manager, the equipment. In a trade where people fear a contractor vanishing, faces work better than stock imagery.
Years in business and projects completed.
Simple specifics that almost nobody states.
Private clients and B2B: why you need two separate paths
This separation is almost never made, and it determines the structure of the site.

A private client is building a house or renovating. They decide emotionally and anxiously, compare several firms, read reviews, fear being cheated, and want to understand the price range and see comparable projects. They need project pages, before-and-after, an explanation of the stages, and a clear enquiry route.

A developer or main contractor is selecting a subcontractor. They look at capacity, licences, insurance, references from comparable projects, timelines, and the ability to hold a schedule. They need figures, not reassurance.
A single page written for both convinces neither: the private client gets lost in the terminology, and the professional can't find the numbers.
Three tiers of a construction company website and what each includes
Simple landing page — €700-1,400
One page: the trades you cover, a few projects, contacts, a form. Right when the task is minimal — an online presence and a link for advertising or a trade platform profile.
What isn't here: separate project and service pages, and therefore no search traffic for specific queries.
Conversion site — from €2,000
The same format built as an acquisition channel: technical SEO and structured data, local markup, a structure designed around the quote request, and readiness for AI search.
Multi-page site — from €2,000

The full structure: trade pages, separate project pages, service areas, a split between private and commercial clients, a structured quote request with drawing upload, and an admin panel for adding projects yourself.
Redesign of an existing site — from €1,000
If the site exists but produces no enquiries, a full rebuild isn't always necessary. Restructuring, adding project pages and local optimisation is often enough.
Simple landing page
— €700-1,400 — Minimal task, traffic from ads — Almost nothing
Conversion site
— from €2,000 — Needs enquiries from search and maps — Local search and map results
Multi-page site
— from €2,000 — Several trades, a portfolio, two client types — Queries by service, project and location
Redesign
— from €1,000 — Site exists but isn't working — Depends on the starting point
What else affects the cost of a construction company website
Photography.
In this field it matters more than copy, and it's a separate line of spending. A shoot covering a few completed projects pays back faster than additional site features.
Sorting the archive.
If projects were photographed unsystematically, part of the work goes into selecting and organising the material.
Language versions.
Relevant for firms serving international clients or hiring crews from abroad.
Timeline.
A relaxed schedule is cheaper than a rushed one, and in construction a site is often wanted "before the season".
What a construction company risks when rebuilding its website
A separate warning based on a real case.

One of my clients in construction had a redesign pushed straight to the live site without checks. Page addresses changed with no redirects, language versions ended up swapped, structured data disappeared. Traffic started falling within two days and hadn't recovered a month later; diagnosis and repair took two weeks.
The conclusion is simple: if a site already has rankings and links,
a rebuild is a migration, not a redraw
. URL structure, markup and redirects are planned before anything changes visually.
How I build websites for construction companies

I combine development and SEO, so the project structure, service area pages and technical base are designed together rather than in sequence. That's also what makes it possible to rebuild an existing site without losing its rankings.

The sequence: we establish which work you want more of and who your client is; I design the structure — projects, trades, service areas, the route to a quote request; then development with local optimisation and markup; then launch and support.
Where to start building a construction company website
Reduced to one principle: a construction company's website works when a client sees a project like their own, understands the price range, and is given grounds to believe you'll finish the job.

Start not with design but by selecting the projects: five to seven builds photographed before and after, with a description of the brief and the decisions made. That's the foundation of the structure and the main source of traffic. Then the trades and the area you genuinely work in.
If you're planning a site or a rebuild of an existing one, write to me and I'll work out what it takes.

children.text: Quick answer:

run a fixed set of ten to twenty-five prompts across ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity, in a clean session, and log five things for each: whether you were named, what was claimed, whether the claim is accurate, which sources were cited, and the date. Run the same set monthly. A single check tells you nothing, because answers vary between runs — the value is in the comparison over time. And before fixing anything, establish whether the error came from a source the assistant retrieved or from the model itself, because only the first kind can be corrected.

Most companies discover what AI assistants say about them by accident: a prospect mentions it, or someone types the company name out of curiosity. By then the answer has been shaping buying decisions for months.
The alternative isn't complicated, but it has to be systematic. Below is the audit method — what to ask, what to record, and how to read what comes back.
Why one check tells you nothing about your AI visibility

The first thing to understand is that assistant answers aren't stable. Ask the same question twice and you may get different companies named, different descriptions and different sources. Ask in a different session, from a different account, or with the phrasing slightly changed, and the variation widens.
That has two consequences for the audit.
The first is that a single run is an impression, not a measurement. Finding your company named once proves it can happen, not that it usually does. Finding it absent once proves nothing at all.

The second is that the unit of measurement has to be a set, not a query. If you run twenty prompts and appear in six answers, that's a number you can compare against next month's six, eleven or two. One prompt gives you nothing to compare.
Building the prompt set for an AI brand audit
The prompt set is the whole method. Build it once, carefully, and then don't change it — changing prompts between runs destroys comparability.
Ten to twenty-five prompts is the workable range. Cover four types:
Branded prompts.
Your company name directly: what it does, what it costs, who runs it, where it operates. These surface factual errors fastest, and they're the ones prospects actually run before a call.
Category prompts.
The service without your name: "who does X for Y in Z". This is where you find out whether you're in consideration at all, and who else is.
Comparison prompts.
Your company against a named competitor, or "alternatives to [competitor]". Uncomfortable, and the most informative.
Problem prompts.
The situation a buyer describes before they know what service they need — with the constraints, the industry and the location a real person would include.

Write them the way a person actually types, not as keyword strings. "We're a dental clinic in Warsaw and our website gets no enquiries, who could help" is a prompt. "dental website development" is a search query, and assistants behave differently with the two.
What to record in an AI brand audit for every prompt
Consistency matters more than volume. For each prompt, log:
Assistant and date — Answers differ by platform and drift over time
Named or not — The primary metric for the whole audit
What was claimed about you — Where factual errors surface
Accurate / outdated / wrong — Errors get triaged by severity, not by order found
Who else was named — Your actual competitive set in AI answers, which often differs from the one you assume
Sources cited — The starting point for any correction
Screenshot — Answers change; without a screenshot you can't prove what was said
A spreadsheet is enough. The tooling matters far less than running the same thing every month.
How to audit ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity separately
Use a clean session.

Log out, or use a private window. A logged-in account carries memory of your previous conversations, and an assistant that has already discussed your company with you will name it far more readily than it would for a stranger.
Run each platform separately.
ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google's AI answers draw on different sources. Presence in one implies nothing about the others, and the same error can exist in one and not another.
Note whether search was used.

ChatGPT answering from its training data and ChatGPT answering after searching the web are effectively two different systems with two different failure modes. If the answer includes citations, the web was used. If it doesn't, you're looking at the model's memory.
Follow the citations.

Gemini and Perplexity show their sources, which makes tracing an error straightforward — open what they cited and you'll usually find the wrong claim sitting there in plain text. ChatGPT often doesn't, in which case you search the incorrect claim itself and see which page ranks for it.
Retrieval error or training-data error: how to tell them apart
This is the distinction that determines whether a fix is possible at all, and most guidance on the topic skips it.
A retrieval error

happens when the assistant searched, found a page containing wrong information, and repeated it. The wrong claim exists somewhere public: an outdated profile, an old press release, a competitor's comparison page, a directory listing nobody has updated in three years. These are correctable, because the source is correctable.
A training-data error

happens when the model states something from its own memory, with no source behind it. Your company was described a certain way in the data the model learned from, and it repeats that. These don't respond to source corrections in the short term — they persist until the model is retrained or until search-grounded answers override them.

How to tell them apart: ask the same question with and without search enabled, where the platform allows it. If the answer changes when the assistant searches, the correct information is retrievable and the problem is that your sources aren't dominant enough. If the wrong claim appears in both, it's in the model.

The practical implication is uncomfortable but worth knowing early: a fraction of what assistants say about you cannot be fixed this quarter, and effort spent trying is wasted. What can be done is making the correct facts so consistently present in retrievable sources that search-grounded answers stay right even while the model's memory lags.
How to read the results of an AI brand audit
Three questions, in order.
Are you named at all?
If you appear in two of twenty answers, the problem is visibility, not accuracy, and the work is the one covered in
the guide on getting recommended by AI assistants
When named, is the description accurate?

Wrong specialisation, outdated services, wrong geography, a price that hasn't been current for two years. Triage these by consequence: anything that affects a buying decision — pricing, capability, whether you serve their industry or country — comes first. Cosmetic staleness can wait.
Which sources keep appearing?
If the same three pages get cited across most answers, those pages are your evidence base, whether you control them or not. That's where correction work starts, and it's often not your own website.
How often to re-run an AI brand audit and what changes to expect

Monthly is the right cadence for most businesses. Weekly produces noise — the natural variation between runs will swamp any real change. Quarterly is too slow to catch an error while it still matters.

Re-run the identical set, in the same conditions, and compare the count of answers naming you and the list of errors still present. Corrections don't appear immediately: source changes have to be recrawled before they can influence an answer, and the lag differs substantially between platforms — retrieval-based systems reflect changes in weeks, while anything grounded in a model's memory may not change at all until a retrain.
Set expectations accordingly. This is a slow-moving measurement, and the value is in the trend across several months, not in any single month's result.
How I run AI brand audits
I combine development and SEO, so an audit doesn't stop at documenting what assistants say — it continues into why, which sources produced it, and what on your site and elsewhere needs to change.

What the work covers: building the prompt set for your market and buyers, running the baseline across platforms, tracing each error to its source, separating what's correctable from what isn't, and setting up the measurement so you can see the trend rather than guess at it.

I'll say the limits plainly: nobody can guarantee what an assistant will say, and some errors won't move until a model is retrained. What can be done is establishing what's actually being said, fixing what's fixable, and knowing which is which.
Where to start auditing what AI says about your company
Reduced to one principle: build the set once, run it in a clean session, log the same fields every time, and compare month to month.

A practical step for today: write ten prompts a buyer of yours would actually type — three branded, three category, two comparison, two problem-based. Run them through ChatGPT and Perplexity in a private window and record what comes back. That hour gives you your baseline, and everything afterwards is measured against it.
If you'd like to know what assistants are currently telling your buyers, write to me and we'll run the audit together.

The beauty industry is one of the few where owners genuinely question whether a website is needed at all: "I already have Instagram, all my work is there." Social media does showcase work better than any website can. But a client looking for a professional for the first time usually goes to Google — "nail salon near me", "cosmetologist in Warsaw", "barber close by". On social media, the people who find you already know you. In search, they don't.
Let's break down what a website for a beauty salon or independent professional actually costs, what each tier includes, and what really drives the price.
What determines the price of a beauty business website
The scale of the business.

An independent professional working alone and a salon with a team of eight are different tasks. A solo professional needs one strong page: work, services, prices, booking. A salon needs separate service pages, staff profiles, scheduling, sometimes multiple locations.
The booking system.

The biggest factor after page count. A simple inquiry form, a messenger link, a full calendar with sync and automatic reminders, integration with the salon's existing CRM — these are very different levels of work.
Online payments and deposits.
If you want to take deposits to reduce no-shows, a payment integration is added — Stripe, PayPal, or a local provider.
The volume of visual content.

Beauty is a visual niche; the gallery isn't decoration here, it's the main argument. The more photo material and the more complex its presentation (galleries by service, before/after, filters), the more work involved.
Local SEO.

For a salon with a physical address, visibility in Google Maps and for "near me" queries is critical. That's a separate layer of technical work: LocalBusiness structured data, correct address and opening-hours markup, pages targeting local queries.
Multiple languages.
In larger cities, beauty clientele often speaks different languages. Language versions with a proper SEO structure for each are additional scope.
Why Instagram doesn't replace a website
Social media and a website solve different problems, and that's worth separating before talking about money.
Instagram shows your work. A website brings new clients from search.
A social profile doesn't rank in Google for "lash lamination Warsaw". A website does — and it brings in people who have never seen you before.
Social media doesn't belong to you.
Algorithms change, reach drops, an account can be blocked by mistake — and an audience built over years disappears in a day. A website is an asset nobody can switch off.
Booking through DMs eats your time.
The "when are you free?" exchange repeats dozens of times a week. A website with a calendar handles that without you — the client sees the open slots and books directly.
Trust is higher.

A client choosing between two professionals will more often pick the one with a website showing transparent prices, reviews, and clear service descriptions. Especially for injectable cosmetology or expensive procedures, where the cost of a bad choice is high.
What every beauty salon website should include
A price list with treatment durations.
Transparent pricing filters out mismatched inquiries and saves reception time. Showing duration helps clients plan their day and cuts down the questions that come before booking.
Online booking.
The central element. The path from "I want this" to "I'm booked" should take a few clicks, with no calls and no messaging.
A gallery of real work.
Not stock photos — your results. In beauty, this is the primary proof of skill.
Staff profiles.
Clients often go to a specific person, not to a salon. Specialist pages with a photo, specialization and portfolio turn a salon from an anonymous place into a set of specific people worth visiting.
Reviews.
Social proof, especially important for first-time clients.
Address, opening hours, map.
Basic information that doubles as a signal for local search.

Simple landing page for an independent professional — €700-1,400

Let me be clear about what this product is, so expectations stay accurate. It's a single page on a solid technical base: custom layout, responsive, fast loading, a contact form, and a basic structure — services, work, contacts. A good solution when the task is minimal: establish an online presence, have a link for your profile bio, collect inquiries from ads.

What isn't here is deep search work. This kind of landing page isn't built to compete in organic results: no expanded structure targeting queries, no optimization layer for AI assistants, no separate service pages. It's an honest budget entry point, not a tool for growth from search.
Personal website with full optimization — from €2,000
The same single-page format, but built as a working acquisition channel. Everything the simple version lacks is added here:
technical SEO and structured data

, AI-search readiness (AEO and GEO) — what makes it possible for ChatGPT or Google AI Overviews to recommend you when someone asks where to get a treatment done; Core Web Vitals optimization; a conversion-focused structure — the visitor's path from first impression to booking; booking integration and, if needed, deposit payments.
The difference between €700 and €2,000 isn't the number of pages — it's whether the site works to bring in clients or simply exists. The first is a business card; the second is a tool.
Salon website with online booking — from €2,000
A multi-page site for a salon with a team

. Everything from the previous tier plus structure: separate pages for each service (which creates entry points from search for specific queries — "lash extensions", "men's haircut" — instead of one general services page), staff profiles, an expanded gallery, a full booking system with calendar sync and reminders, local SEO with LocalBusiness markup for Google Maps visibility, and an admin panel where reception can change prices, add services and update photos independently.
The final cost depends on the number of services and staff, the complexity of the booking system, and whether language versions are needed — describe your salon and I'll prepare a quote.
What else affects the final cost
Content.

Texts and photos — yours, or you need help. In beauty, photo quality is critical: weak images undercut even an excellent site, so it's sometimes wiser to invest in a photo session than in extra features.
Accepting payments.
A payment integration for deposits is separate scope, but it pays for itself by reducing no-shows.
Multiple languages.
Each language version means not just translation but a separate SEO structure.
Timeline.
A relaxed schedule is more economical than a rushed one.
How I build websites for beauty businesses

I combine development with SEO/AEO/GEO optimization: the site is built from the start so that it gets found — both through Google and through the AI assistants people increasingly ask for recommendations.

I have hands-on experience in this niche: I built a landing page for a professional training course in the beauty field — with custom design, mobile optimization, and Stripe integration for taking course payments directly on the site.

Services, staff, clients, how booking currently works.

The client's path from search to booking, conversion points, service structure aligned to search queries.

children.text: Quick answer:

comparing quotes by price is meaningless, because they contain different scopes of work. Before signing, establish five things: who will own the domain, hosting and code; what exactly is included and what will turn out to be an extra; what the site is built on and whether another developer could take it over; what happens after launch; and whether there's a contract with the scope written down. A good sign is a contractor who asks about your business rather than only about page counts.

Quotes for the same phrase — "build me a website" — range from a few hundred to tens of thousands. That's disorienting, and it pushes people towards a simple decision: take the cheapest, or take whoever has the prettiest portfolio. Both are poor criteria, because neither answers the real question: what exactly will you get, and what happens to it a year from now.
Below is what to establish before signing, and the signs that suggest walking away.
Who owns the domain, hosting and code after the site is delivered
I start here because it's the one item that can cost you the entire site.

"We'll handle everything" looks convenient, and often it is. The problem arises when the domain is registered to the contractor, the hosting is paid from their account, and the source code lives in their repository. Formally, the site isn't yours. While the relationship is good, nobody notices. When you decide to change contractor, or receive a renewal invoice at three times the market rate, your negotiating position turns out to be weak.

How it should be: the domain registered to you or your company, hosting paid from your account or with full administrative access on your side, and the code and content yours from the moment of payment. Access handed over as a complete set, not "as needed".
The question worth asking word for word: can I take the site elsewhere at any point, and what would that require? The answer tells you more about a contractor than their portfolio does.
What's included in the price and what turns out to be an extra
The second reason price comparison fails: the same figure can cover very different scopes.

What to check in every quote, point by point: custom design or a template, copy — yours or theirs, images and their licensing, hosting and SSL setup, basic technical optimisation, language versions, training on the admin panel, how many rounds of revisions are included, and migration from an old site with URLs preserved.
Each of those is usually missing from a cheap quote and reappears later as an extra. What was cheaper wasn't the quote — it was its first line.

Practical advice: ask not for a price but for the scope in writing. Two quotes reduced to the same scope can be compared honestly — and it often turns out the price difference was a difference in contents.
What the site is built on and whether another developer can take it over
The technology itself isn't a quality criterion: a well-built WordPress site beats a badly built one on a modern framework. What matters is how standard the solution is.

The problematic variants: a proprietary system only that contractor knows; a builder with closed export that the site can't be taken out of; a stack of paid plugins you pay for annually. What they have in common is that you can't leave the contractor or the platform without a rebuild.
The question: if we ended the relationship tomorrow, could another developer pick this up, and what would they need? A clear answer here matters more than how fashionable the stack sounds.
How to verify a web developer's portfolio
Attractive previews tell you nothing. What needs checking is live sites, and it takes twenty minutes.

Open several projects from links rather than images. Do the sites still exist — part of most portfolios has long been taken down. Check mobile speed with any public tool. See whether those sites are found in search for their services, not just for the company name. And note whether any project resembles yours in complexity, rather than in industry.
Separately: ask what exactly the contractor did on each project. In agencies and teams the same case study circulates through everyone's portfolio, and each person's role in it was different.
What questions to ask a web developer before signing
Who owns the domain, hosting, code
— You do, access handed over in full — "We keep it all with us, it's easier"
What's included in the price
— A written list of work — A price with no scope, "all inclusive"
What do you build on
— A standard solution, choice explained — A proprietary, closed system
What happens after launch
— Support terms and response times — "We'll sort that out later"
Timeline
— Realistic, broken into stages — Half the time everyone else quoted
Revisions
— An agreed number of rounds — Not discussed until there's a conflict
Search rankings
— Explains they can't be guaranteed — Promises first place
My business
— Asks about clients and goals — Asks only about page counts

That last row is the most underrated signal. A contractor who opens with questions about your clients and where enquiries currently come from will build a tool. One who asks only about page counts and preferred styling will build a picture.
Red flags when choosing a website contractor
Guaranteed first place in search.
Positions depend on competition and algorithms; they can be influenced, not guaranteed. A promise like that means either a misunderstanding of the field or an expectation that you won't notice.
No contract and no written scope.
Verbal agreements can't be enforced, and an argument about whether a feature was included is never settled in your favour.
A price quoted without questions about the task.
An exact figure given before establishing what's needed means a template — a template may fit, but it's worth knowing in advance.
A timeline noticeably shorter than everyone else's.
Either the scope is missing something the others include, or the deadline won't hold.
Answers you can't follow.
A professional explains simply because they understand the subject. Jargon with no visible meaning behind it more often covers emptiness than depth.
Not a single live site in the portfolio
, only mockups and previews.
What web development costs: reference points
To have something to compare quotes against, it helps to know the order of magnitude.
A simple landing page — €700-1,400.
A conversion landing page with full search and AI optimisation — from €2,000. A multi-page business site — from €2,000. A redesign of an existing site — from €1,000.

A quote noticeably below the lower bound usually means a template with standard content. That isn't always bad: if the task is minimal, a template can be the right answer. It's bad when a template is priced like bespoke work, or sold for a task it can't solve.
How to tell you don't need a developer at all
A separate point, and one rarely found in articles written by contractors.
Sometimes the task is solved by a website builder over a weekend and hiring anyone makes no sense: you're testing an idea, you need a business card, and search isn't part of the plan.
A good contractor will say exactly that.

It's easy to test. Describe the task honestly, including a modest budget and your uncertainty, and watch the response. Someone who proposes reducing the scope, or says plainly that a simpler solution will do, is more reliable than someone who proposes the maximum package in every situation.
The related question — freelancer or agency — I cover in a separate article, because it deserves a proper comparison.
How I work
I'll say it plainly: I'm an interested party in this text, which is why the checklist above is written so it can be used to assess any contractor, including me.

My answers to the same questions: the domain, hosting, code and content belong to the client, and access is handed over in full. I work on standard solutions — Next.js and WordPress without page builders — so another developer can take the site over. Scope is written down before work starts. I don't guarantee search positions and I explain what they depend on. And if a task can be solved more simply and cheaply than full development, I say so.
I combine development and SEO, so technical optimisation is built in during the work rather than bolted on afterwards by a separate contractor.
Where to start choosing a web developer
Reduced to one principle: compare scopes rather than prices, and settle the ownership question before anything is paid.

The sequence is simple. Write the task down: why you need the site, who your clients are, where enquiries come from now, what budget and timeline you have. Send the same text to several contractors. Compare not the figures but what's inside them, and what questions came back. Check the live sites in their portfolios. Only then discuss price.
If you'd like to talk through your own project, write to me and we'll work out what you actually need.

children.text: Quick answer:

the question isn't who's better but which risk you can accept. With a freelancer you speak directly to the person doing the work and pay no structural markup, but you depend on one individual: illness, another project or leaving the market stops everything. An agency provides continuity, several specialists working in parallel and formal guarantees, but charges a markup and often staffs the project with someone other than whoever sold it. For a typical company website the balance usually favours a freelancer; for a large multi-stream project, an agency.

Most comparisons on this subject are written either by an agency or by someone working on their own, and their conclusions are predictable. I work on my own, so I'll say it upfront: I have an obvious interest here. What follows is an attempt to describe the real differences, including the ones where I'm the weaker side.
Freelancer, sole trader and agency: why the terms get confused
Before comparing anything, three different things need separating, because they're constantly conflated in this discussion.
A contractor from a gig platform.
Work without a contract, payment by agreement, accountability limited to a profile rating. That's the image the word "freelancer" usually carries, and it's what clients are wary of.
A registered specialist working alone.

A registered business, contracts, invoices, taxes, warranties and accountability for the result — everything a company has, with one person doing the work. Formally it is a company, just a one-person one.
An agency.
A team, an account manager, a structure, several specialists on one project.

The real difference doesn't run between "freelancer" and "company" — it runs between one contractor and a team. Whether the relationship is formalised is a separate question, and worth establishing with any type of supplier: is there a contract, who carries liability, how are invoices issued. So from here on I compare two working models rather than legal forms.
What actually differs between one contractor and an agency
The difference isn't quality, and it isn't price as such. It's four things.
Who you talk to.

With a freelancer, the person who designs and writes the code. Your comments go straight to the person acting on them. At an agency you speak to an account manager who passes work along. That isn't necessarily bad — the manager takes coordination off your hands. But every intermediary loses some of the meaning.
What happens if the person doing the work drops out.

The key difference. A freelancer is a single point of failure: illness, a large project, leaving the market — and your site stops. At an agency the project transfers to another specialist. Slower and with lost context, but it doesn't halt.
Who actually does the work.
With a freelancer it's obvious. At an agency a senior sells and a more junior specialist frequently builds. That's a normal model, but it's worth knowing about and asking directly.
What you're paying for.

An agency's price contains structure: an account manager, an office, sales, administration. Sometimes that's justified — you're paying for coordination and continuity. Sometimes it's a markup for something your project doesn't need.
When hiring a freelancer for a website makes more sense
The task fits in one head.
A company site, a landing page, a catalogue, a blog with a considered structure — a typical scope one experienced person builds end to end, with no losses in handovers between specialists.
Direct conversation with the builder matters.
Particularly if you understand the subject yourself and want to discuss decisions rather than pass wishes through a manager.
The budget is limited but the task isn't minimal.
Without a structural markup, the same money usually buys more work.
You need combined skills in one person.

Development and SEO together, for example. At an agency that's two departments and a handover between them; with one person it's a single piece of work, and technical optimisation gets built in rather than bolted on afterwards.
When an agency is the better choice
The project is large and multi-part.
A portal, a complex store, a system with integrations where several specialists need to work simultaneously. One person will either fail or take four times as long.
Many parallel streams are needed.
Design, development, content, advertising, analytics — at the same time and continuously.
Continuity is critical.
If the site is a production system whose downtime costs money, you need a supplier that doesn't disappear along with one individual.
There are formal requirements.
Tenders, large corporate procurement, requirements about a supplier's legal form and insurance.
Nobody internally can run the project.
An agency's manager solves a real problem — that's what the markup buys.
Freelancer and agency compared across key criteria
Who you communicate with
— The person doing the work — An account manager
Who performs the work
— The person you chose — Not always the one who sold it
If they drop out
— The project stops — Transfers to another specialist
Parallel workstreams
— Limited to one person — Several specialists at once
Price at equal scope
— Lower, no structural markup — Higher, includes coordination
Speed of decisions
— High, one person decides — Lower, internal sign-off
Formal guarantees
— Depend on the contract — Usually stronger
Depth in a narrow field
— Often greater — Depends who lands on the project
How to reduce the risk of working with a freelancer
The risk is real, and it's mitigated by procedure rather than by trust.
Own everything.
Domain and hosting registered to you, code and content yours, access handed over in full. Then a contractor disappearing is an inconvenience rather than a catastrophe.
A standard stack.
If the site is built on widely used solutions, any other developer can pick it up. A contractor's proprietary system turns a single point of failure into a dead end.
Documentation and handover.
Admin panel instructions, credentials, backups. A good contractor leaves these by default.
Payment in stages.
Not the whole budget up front and not all at the end — tying payments to milestones protects both sides.
Ask directly about workload.
How many projects are running in parallel, and what happens to your timeline if another large one arrives. The answer reveals both honesty and real availability.
Scope in writing.
Verbal agreements are the source of most conflicts, whatever type of contractor you choose.
How to reduce the risk of working with an agency
Ask who specifically will do the work.
Not the team's name but the roles and experience of the people on your project. And ask to speak to whoever will build it, not just the account manager.
Establish what happens if staff change.
People move within agencies; what matters is that this doesn't mean lost context and half the work redone.
Check whether your project fits their scale.
A small site at a large agency risks sitting at the bottom of the priority list.
Break the quote down by line.
A structural markup is justified when the structure works on your project. If there's nothing to coordinate, you're paying for air.
The same ownership question.
Domain, hosting, code and access should be yours regardless of who builds the site.
What a website costs with a freelancer versus an agency
Direct price comparison is misleading, because the scopes differ. But the order of magnitude helps:
a simple landing page — €700-1,400; a conversion landing page with full optimisation — from €2,000; a multi-page business site — from €2,000; a redesign — from €1,000

An agency at the same scope is usually more expensive, and that isn't inflation: the price includes coordination, an account manager and a continuity guarantee. The question is whether you need those line items. For a five-to-fifteen page company site, usually not. For a portal with integrations, almost certainly yes.
Separately:
a price well below market from any type of contractor means a template, a reduced scope, or work without a contract
. That isn't always bad, but it should be a conscious choice.
How to choose between a freelancer and an agency: four questions
How many streams need running at once?
One — a freelancer. Three or more, continuously — an agency.
What happens if the site stalls for two weeks?
Nothing serious — the freelancer risk is acceptable. Financial losses — you need continuity.
Do you have someone to run the project?
If not, and you don't want to do it yourself, an agency's manager solves a genuine problem.
Do you need combined skills or a range of them?
Development plus SEO in one head works better than two departments. Design plus development plus advertising plus analytics simultaneously is a job for a team.
The related question — how to assess a specific contractor of either type, what to ask and what to look for in a portfolio — I cover in a separate article on choosing a web developer.
How I work

I'm not a freelancer in the sense the word usually carries: I run a registered business, work on contracts, issue invoices and carry accountability for the result. Structurally I'm one specialist rather than a team — and that means specific things, including uncomfortable ones.

What you get: a direct conversation with me, no account manager and no losses in handover; development and SEO in one person, so technical optimisation is built in during the work; no markup for structure.

What you accept as risk: I'm one person. If I fall ill or take on a large project, your timeline may shift. That's precisely why with me the domain, hosting, code and content belong to the client, the stack is standard — Next.js and WordPress without page builders — and access and documentation are handed over in full. It doesn't remove the risk, but it turns it from a dead end into an inconvenience.
And honestly about the limits: if your project needs several specialists working simultaneously and continuously, I'll say so — that's a job for a team.
Where to start choosing between a freelancer and an agency

Reduced to one principle: describe the project and your continuity requirements first, then choose the type of contractor. The reverse — picking a format and then fitting the task to it — is the most common mistake.

A practical step: write one page covering what you need, how many streams run in parallel, what your budget is, and what happens if work stops for two weeks. That document is usually enough to make the answer obvious — and it's the same document you'll use to request quotes.
If you'd like to talk through your own project, write to me and we'll work out what suits it.

children.text: Quick answer:

for most business websites WordPress is enough — provided it's built on a custom theme rather than a page builder carrying twenty plugins. A modern framework such as Next.js is justified when speed is critical, when you need non-standard integrations, complex multilingual structure, or a site meant to grow for years. But the main question isn't the platform. It's how the platform is built and what ownership costs over three years.

The question is usually framed as a choice between two things: WordPress or a custom build. That framing misses the point, because one WordPress site is not like another. A site assembled on a page builder with thirty plugins and a site built on a custom theme written for the job are two different products — differing from each other more than the second differs from a framework.
So it's more honest to compare three options rather than two. Here's how they differ and what each actually costs.
Three options rather than two: how the platforms really differ
WordPress on a page builder.

A ready-made theme plus Elementor or similar, plus a plugin for every function. Fast, cheap to start, usable without a developer. The price is page weight: the builder loads code for every eventuality, and speed drops regardless of hosting quality.
WordPress on a custom theme.

The same WordPress, but with a theme written for the job — no builder, no plugin pile-up. Only what's needed gets loaded. From the owner's side everything is familiar: the same admin panel, the same text and images, edited the same way.
A modern framework with a separate content system.
The site is built for the job on Next.js or similar, with content managed in a separate system. Maximum speed and control, minimal maintenance, a higher budget threshold.

The key conclusion: the gap between the first and second options is wider than the gap between the second and third. Most complaints about WordPress are complaints about the first option, not about the platform.
When WordPress is enough for a business website
Content changes often and in-house.
A vast ecosystem, a familiar panel, any staff member can manage it. That's a genuine advantage, not a compromise.
You need standard functionality.
A blog, forms, a catalogue, a simple store, integrations with popular services — all already written and proven.
Ease of handover matters.
There are a great many developers who work with WordPress.
If you part ways with a contractor, replacing them is easier than with any other solution.
The budget is limited and the task is standard.
A five-to-fifteen page company site with a blog, on a custom theme, is a sensible choice with nothing to overpay for.
The caveat that decides everything: this applies to WordPress on a custom theme. The same site assembled on a builder inherits every problem the platform gets criticised for.
Where WordPress hits its ceiling: speed, security and maintenance
Speed.

Every plugin adds its own scripts and styles, often on all pages including those where the function isn't used. Twenty plugins means twenty sets of code on every load. Hence the drop in Core Web Vitals, which neither hosting nor caching fully cures.
Maintenance as a standing cost.

The core and plugins need regular updates: an un-updated site becomes vulnerable, and a failed update breaks the layout. Add backups and monitoring. This isn't a one-off cost but a monthly load — paid either in money or in someone's time.
Security.
Its popularity makes WordPress the primary target of automated attacks. The issue isn't the platform itself but that a vulnerable plugin gets found faster than you learn it exists.
Paid plugins.
Functions that look free often turn out to be subscriptions, and across three years they add up to a figure nobody considered at launch.
When a modern framework like Next.js is the better choice
Speed is critical.

If the site lives on search and conversion, the Core Web Vitals difference pays for itself. On a framework only what's needed loads, and the result is stable rather than clawed back through optimisation.
You need non-standard integrations.
Connections to internal systems, unusual calculations, client portals — where WordPress needs workarounds, a framework needs code.
Complex multilingual structure.
Several markets with different page structures, rather than translated copies of one site.
The site is meant to grow for years.
The longer the horizon, the clearer the difference in cost of ownership: no plugins to police, no licences, maintenance reduced to hosting.
Minimal upkeep matters.
If nobody will watch for updates, that's a serious argument.
Against: a higher budget threshold, and no reason to solve a simple task with a solution like this.
Platforms compared across key criteria
Build cost
— Lowest — Middle — Higher
Loading speed
— Low — High — Maximum
Updating content
— Simple — Simple — Simple, panel configured separately
Ongoing maintenance
— Required — Required — Minimal
Plugins and licences
— Many, often paid — Minimal — None
Risk on updates
— High — Moderate — Low
Who can take it over
— Almost anyone — Almost anyone — A developer on that stack
Non-standard features
— Via workarounds — Limited — No limits
What owning a website costs over three years
Comparing build prices is the same mistake as comparing car prices without fuel and servicing.
Build: a simple landing page — €700-1,400; a conversion landing page with full optimisation — from €2,000; a multi-page site — from €2,000.

Then comes what usually doesn't reach the quote. With WordPress that's regular technical maintenance, subscriptions to paid plugins, fixing the aftermath of failed updates and, with bad luck, recovering from a compromise. With a framework, maintenance usually reduces to hosting, but changes to functionality need a developer — you can't rewire the logic yourself.
The practical conclusion: over a one-year horizon WordPress is cheaper; over three to five years the gap narrows; and with high traffic and demanding speed requirements it can reverse.
What practice on both solutions shows
I work with both, so the comparison isn't theoretical.
I moved a Warsaw wheel restoration workshop off an ageing platform
onto a
custom WordPress theme
— no builder, no heavy plugins.
Mobile performance went from around 50 to 92, the site runs in four languages, and the staff change prices and add services themselves.
It's an example of WordPress built properly having nothing to do with what the platform gets criticised for.
My own site I built on
Next.js with a separate content management system
, in three locales. The task there was different: speed, precise work with markup, and a structure designed for search engines and AI assistants.
The conclusion from both: the platform is chosen for the task, and a badly built site on a modern framework loses to a well-built one on WordPress.
How to choose a platform for your website: four questions
Who will change the content, and how often?
Daily and in-house — WordPress. Once a quarter — the platform doesn't matter much.
Does the site earn from search?
If so, speed and the technical base outweigh editing convenience, and a framework is justified.
Are there non-standard features and integrations?
Calculations, client portals, connections to internal systems tip the balance towards a framework.
Who will look after the site?
If nobody will, having no mandatory updates is a serious argument.
And the question that outweighs all four: who is going to build it. Good work on WordPress beats poor work on any framework, and the reverse.
How I choose the platform for a project

I work with both and choose by the task rather than by habit. WordPress — on a custom theme, without builders or unnecessary plugins, so you get both the convenience of the panel and the speed. Next.js with a separate content system — where maximum performance, complex structure or unusual logic is needed.
I combine development and SEO, so the platform decision accounts for how the site will be found, not only how it will look. And if the task can be solved more simply and cheaply, I say so.
Where to start choosing a platform for a business website
Reduced to one principle: choose not a platform but a combination of the task, the horizon, and who will run the site afterwards.

A practical step: answer the four questions above in writing and add a fifth — what should exist on the site in two years. That answer often decides it, because building the structure in now is cheaper than rebuilding later.
If you'd like to work out what suits your project, write to me and we'll go through it.

excerpt: A comparison of platforms for a business website: WordPress on a page builder, WordPress on a custom theme, and a modern framework. What costs more over three years, and why the platform isn't the main question.

children.text: Quick answer:

a one-time SEO audit costs from €250. Monthly support for a small business starts from €800/month with a minimum 3-6 month commitment. SEO for competitive niches starts from €1,300/month, minimum six months. Full project management by one specialist, including technical code changes and marketing, is €3,000/month. The final cost depends on niche competition, the site's current state, and exactly what's included in the work.

"How much does SEO cost" sounds like a simple question, and the answer is almost never a single number. SEO isn't a one-off service like painting a fence — it's an ongoing process, and its price is shaped the same way any expert work is priced: by scope, complexity, and competition. In this guide I break down what SEO pricing is made of, what support tiers exist, and what to watch for when choosing who to work with — no fluff.
What determines the price of SEO

The price range for SEO on the market is huge — from a few hundred euros a month with a freelancer to tens of thousands with an agency. The reason isn't overcharging or undercharging — it's that "SEO" covers tasks of vastly different scale.
Niche competition.
Ranking a local plumbing company and ranking a real estate site in an international market are tasks of a completely different order.
The more strong competitors already occupy the search results, the more work it takes to outrank them, and the higher the price.
The site's current state.
If a site is new or has technical problems (poor structure, indexing errors, slow loading), those fundamental obstacles need fixing first before growth work can begin. That adds scope at the start.
Scope and complexity of the technical work.
Speed audits, structure, keyword research, content strategy, link work, technical optimization — each component takes specialist time.
Who does the work.

An SEO specialist without development skills can give recommendations but can't implement them — you still need a developer who understands the task and executes it. A specialist who covers both roles closes the gap between "what needs to happen" and "what actually gets done," and that changes the economics: you pay one person instead of coordinating two.
The format of collaboration.
A one-time audit, monthly support across a few tasks, or full project management are different levels of involvement, and the price reflects that difference.
Why SEO is a process, not a one-off service

It's worth understanding one principle before comparing prices: SEO doesn't produce results in a week. Search engines need to re-crawl changes and accumulate trust signals for a site, and that takes months, not days. That's why SEO work almost always comes with a minimum commitment period — not because someone wants to lock you in longer, but because a meaningful result physically can't appear sooner. Any offer promising a quick ranking jump in a week or two is worth treating with suspicion — it's either inexperience or manipulative tactics that can hurt the site long-term.
How much an SEO audit and consultation cost
Free consultation — 15-30 minutes

The first step before any investment. We discuss your site and business, I give you an honest read on whether SEO makes sense for your situation, and explain realistic scenarios — not sell a service for the sake of selling one.
SEO audit — from €250

An audit isn't a generic report with recommendations like "improve content" and "optimize speed" that say nothing specific. A full audit includes: technical diagnostics (speed, indexing errors, structure), an assessment of search visibility and keyword opportunity, competitor analysis, and — most importantly — a concrete, prioritized action plan: what to do first, what can wait. It's one-time work, but it's often a sensible first step before a bigger investment: you get a clear picture of where the site is losing rankings and traffic, and you decide, with real information, whether to go further.
How much monthly SEO support costs
For small and medium businesses — from €800/month

Suited to service businesses, local niches, and sites where the goal is a steady stream of inquiries rather than fighting for the market's most expensive keywords. The minimum commitment is 3-6 months, because that's roughly how long it takes for a visible effect to build up. Scope includes: technical and SEO audit, keyword optimization, structural and content improvements, results analysis and next-step recommendations.
For competitive niches — from €1,300/month

Suited to businesses in highly competitive niches that need steady, measurable ranking growth against strong market players. Minimum commitment is 6 months. This requires more: deeper technical optimization, a more active content strategy, and more attention to signals that would be overkill in a calmer niche. Competitive work costs more precisely because there are more competitors, and each of them is already doing something for their own rankings.
Full project management — €3,000/month

This isn't the next intensity tier — it's a different way of working. One specialist fully owns the growth channel through the site: SEO strategy and execution, content, technical improvements and code changes, marketing coordination. In effect, it replaces a team of an SEO specialist, a developer and a marketer with one person who understands the whole picture and doesn't lose time handing tasks between people. For a business where the site is the primary client-acquisition channel rather than one of many, this format often turns out not more expensive but cheaper than maintaining or coordinating several contractors — and noticeably faster to execute, since there's no waiting for an SEO recommendation to reach a developer and land in their queue.
One-time SEO services — from €250 to €700

You don't always need an ongoing format. Sometimes targeted work is enough: a check after technical changes to the site, a consultation on a specific question, a one-off optimization of a page for target keywords. One-time services don't replace ongoing SEO, but they can be a sensible first step or a targeted fix for a specific problem.
Why cheap SEO often costs more in the end
The temptation to save money on SEO is understandable, but this is a place where it's especially easy to lose more than you save. Let's look at exactly where.
SEO without technical understanding.

A specialist who gives recommendations but can't implement them creates a gap: recommendations exist, execution doesn't, because a developer either doesn't fully understand the task or puts it in a queue for weeks. The time between diagnosis and action is lost rankings.
Aggressive tactics for a quick result.

Some providers promise fast growth through methods search engines recognize as manipulation — sooner or later this leads to penalties, and recovering from those takes significantly more time and money than honest SEO would have cost from the start.
No transparent reporting.

Cheap offers often don't include clear reporting on what's being done and why. Without that, there's no way to tell whether the strategy is working, and it's easy to keep paying for inactivity for months.
Scattered one-off work without a strategy.

Chaotic, piecemeal fixes without an overall picture can even backfire — for example, optimizing one page for the same keywords already targeted by another page on the same site creates internal competition between your own pages, and both lose ground instead of one strong page winning.
Quality SEO costs more because you're paying for expertise that brings measurable growth, not the appearance of activity.
How I run SEO work
I combine SEO expertise with technical development

— a rare combination that closes the main gap in classic SEO: between what needs to happen and what's actually implemented on the site. I don't just give recommendations — I implement them myself: technical fixes, code changes, structural changes — with no developer queue and no details lost in translation between people.
The work also includes optimization for
the newer layer of search — AEO and GEO

, meaning the site's readiness to be understood and recommended by AI assistants like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews. This isn't theory — clients have already found me through ChatGPT itself. People increasingly search beyond Google alone, and a site needs to be technically ready for both channels.
How the work is structured:
1. Free consultation.
We discuss your site, business, and realistic scenarios.
2. Audit.
Full technical and SEO diagnostics with a concrete action plan.
3. Strategy and execution.
Depending on the format — targeted work or ongoing support with a full cycle from analysis to implementation.
4. Analysis and growth.
Regular results review, strategy adjustments, transparent reporting on what was done and why.

A one-time SEO audit costs from €250. Monthly support for a small or medium business starts from €800/month with a minimum 3-6 month commitment. SEO for competitive niches starts from €1,300/month, minimum six months. Full project management by one specialist, including technical code changes and marketing, is €3,000/month. The exact cost depends on niche competition and the site's current state — describe your situation and I'll prepare a quote.
